methods.label: Test all four claims with a counterexample
methods.explanation:
Each proposed relation would have to follow for every allowed interior point. We can reject the claims by constructing one configuration where they fail.

Take
\[
A=(0,0),\quad B=(12,0),\quad C=(0,12),\quad P=(3,3).
\]
The point \(P\) is inside the triangle because its coordinates are positive and \(3+3<12\). Let \(AP,BP,CP\) meet the opposite sides at \(D,E,F\), respectively. These three lines have equations \(y=x\), \(x+3y=12\), and \(3x+y=12\), so
\[
D=(6,6),\qquad E=(0,4),\qquad F=(4,0).
\]
The sections \(AFP\) and \(CDP\) are an opposite pair around \(P\).

Their squared side lengths are
\[
AF^2=16,\quad FP^2=10,\quad PA^2=18,
\]
\[
CD^2=72,\quad DP^2=18,\quad PC^2=90.
\]
Triangle \(CDP\) is right because \(72+18=90\). Triangle \(AFP\) is not right: its largest squared side, \(18\), is not \(16+10\). Thus these opposite triangles are neither similar nor congruent, rejecting A and B.

Their areas also differ:
\[
[AFP]=\frac12\cdot4\cdot3=6,
\qquad
[CDP]=\frac12\sqrt{72}\sqrt{18}=18.
\]
This rejects C.

Finally, two of the quadrilateral regions are \(AFPE\) and \(BDPF\). Their squared side lengths, in boundary order, are
\[
(16,10,10,16)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(72,18,10,64).
\]
The first quadrilateral has equal adjacent sides, while all four sides of the second have different lengths. Similarity preserves equality between side lengths, so these quadrilaterals cannot be similar. This rejects D.

All four relations fail in a valid configuration. Therefore none is guaranteed, and the answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
